_desc: How to backpack Italy on the classic Cities of Art route: Rome, Florence and Venice by train in 7 to 10 days. Budget tips, hostels and how to plan it.
b1: Backpacking Italy: The Classic Rome–Florence–Venice Route
b2: By WoW Train · July 2026 · 6 min read
b3: If it's your first time backpacking Italy, one route earns its reputation more than any other: the Cities of Art circuit — Rome, Florence and Venice, connected by fast trains, packed with the monuments and museums that define the country. It's the itinerary every guidebook starts with, and for good reason.
b4: Why this is the route to start with
b5: Rome, Florence and Venice sit on the same high-speed rail corridor, each about 1-2 hours apart, and every station drops you in the historic centre — no airport transfers, no rental car, no long bus rides. For a backpacker moving with one bag and a loose budget, that's the whole appeal: pack up, walk to the station, and you're in the next city before lunch.
b6: Between the three cities you get the Colosseum and the Vatican, the birthplace of the Renaissance, and a city built entirely on water — three completely different Italys in one trip.
b8: 7 days (tight but doable): 2 in Rome, 2 in Florence, 2 in Venice, 1 for travel days.
b9: 10 days (comfortable): 3 in Rome, 2-3 in Florence, 3 in Venice — enough to actually rest between museums.
b10: Rome deserves the extra day if you can spare it — between the Colosseum, the Forum and the Vatican Museums, it's easy to burn through two full days just on the big three.
b12: Base yourself near Roma Termini, the main station — it keeps every onward train a short walk away and puts you close to hostels in the San Lorenzo and Esquilino neighbourhoods, both known for being backpacker-friendly and walkable to the centre. Hit the Colosseum and Forum early to beat the heat and the queues, and book the Vatican Museums in advance online — the walk-up line can eat half a day.
b14: A Frecciarossa or Italo high-speed train covers Rome to Florence in about 1h 30m, arriving at Firenze Santa Maria Novella — a 10-minute walk from the Duomo. Book a few weeks ahead for the cheapest fares; last-minute tickets on this route can cost more than double.
b16: Florence rewards slow walking more than any checklist. The Duomo, the Uffizi, the Ponte Vecchio and a sunset at Piazzale Michelangelo are the essentials, but the whole historic centre fits inside a couple of kilometres — you won't need transit inside the city, which keeps costs down.
b18: Another high-speed hop, roughly 2 hours direct on Frecciarossa or Italo, landing at Venezia Santa Lucia — step outside and the Grand Canal is right there. No cars are allowed on the islands, so from the station it's on foot or by vaporetto (water bus) the rest of the way.
b20: Venice is the priciest stop on this route, so it pays to plan. Stay in Cannaregio or on the mainland in Mestre (a short train ride from Santa Lucia) for cheaper beds, walk instead of taking the vaporetto whenever the distance allows, and eat where the locals do — a few streets back from St Mark's Square, prices drop fast.
b21: Keeping the trip on a backpacker budget
b22: Book high-speed trains 3-6 weeks ahead. Frecciarossa and Italo use dynamic pricing — the earlier you book, the cheaper the fare.
b23: Hostels over hotels. All three cities have well-reviewed hostels in walking distance of the main sights, usually far cheaper than a hotel room.
b24: City centre stations mean no transfer costs. Unlike flying between cities, there's no taxi or shuttle to budget for at either end.
b25: Skip-the-line tickets for the Vatican and Uffizi cost a bit more but save hours you'd otherwise spend queuing — often worth it on a short trip.
b26: Carry one bag you can walk with. Italian train stations aren't always step-free, and cobblestone streets in Florence and Venice aren't kind to wheeled luggage.
b28: Booked ahead, the two high-speed legs (Rome–Florence and Florence–Venice) typically run around €40–€70 total per person — a small slice of the trip compared to accommodation, and far cheaper than flying between three cities.
b29: Juggling three cities, several train operators and live departure times is the one part of backpacking Italy that can get messy. That's exactly what WoW Train is built for: live schedules and fares across Trenitalia, Italo and every other European railway, in one app, in your language.
b31: Plan your Italy route, see live schedules, and book through verified partners.
b33: How many days do you need to backpack the Cities of Art route in Italy?
b34: 7 to 10 days is the classic window: 2-3 in Rome, 2 in Florence, 2-3 in Venice, plus travel days. A week works if you move fast; 10 days lets you breathe.
b35: Is Italy easy to backpack by train?
b36: Yes — Rome, Florence and Venice are connected by frequent high-speed trains (Frecciarossa, Italo) of 1-2 hours each, and every station is in the city centre, so there's no airport transfer to plan around.
